s: Charon is a sordid god
q: A sordid god: down from his hoary chin A length of beard descends, uncomb’d, unclean;

s: Aeneas is son of Anchises
q: “Son of Anchises, offspring of the gods,”

s: Charon has a hoary beard (uncombed and unclean)
q: A sordid god: down from his hoary chin A length of beard descends, uncomb’d, unclean;

s: Charon refuses to carry living bodies (across the Styx)
q: My boat conveys no living bodies o’er;

s: Cerberus is a triple porter (of the Stygian sound)
q: No sooner landed, in his den they found The triple porter of the Stygian sound, Grim Cerberus,

s: Cerberus has three mouths (enormous and ravenous)
q: With three enormous mouths he gapes; and straight, With hunger press’d, devours the pleasing bait.

s: Palinurus is a new-admitted ghost (fresh from life)
q: Amidst the spirits, Palinurus press’d, Yet fresh from life, a new-admitted guest,

s: Palinurus is overcome by fatal sleep
q: My wearied eyes were seiz’d with fatal sleep. I fell; and, with my weight, the helm constrain’d Was drawn along, which yet my gripe retain’d.

s: death of Palinurus is caused by Sleep (while he is steering)
q: My wearied eyes were seiz’d with fatal sleep. I fell; and, with my weight, the helm constrain’d

s: Aeneas is famed for filial love
q: Much fam’d for arms, and more for filial love,

s: the golden bough is a destined offering (for Pluto’s queen)
q: Admir’d the destin’d off’ring to his queen;

s: the golden bough must be fixed high (before the farther way)
q: Before our farther way the Fates allow, Here must we fix on high the golden bough.”

s: the Furies punish the guilty (with whips and snakes)
q: Straight, o’er the guilty ghost, the Fury shakes The sounding whip and brandishes her snakes,

s: Dido is a Phoenician queen (among the dead)
q: Not far from these Phoenician Dido stood,

s: Dido is dead by suicide (after Aeneas’s departure)
q: Unhappy queen! then is the common breath Of rumour true, in your reported death,

s: Dido rejects Aeneas (with disdain in the Underworld)
q: Disdainfully she look’d; then turning round, But fix’d her eyes unmov’d upon the ground,

s: Aeneas possesses Aeneas's sword (shining and unsheathed)
q: The chief unsheath’d his shining steel, prepar’d, Tho’ seiz’d with sudden fear, to force the guard,

s: Deiphobus has a mutilated body (with wounds to face and limbs)
q: Whose face and limbs were one continued wound: Dishonest, with lopp’d arms, the youth appears, Spoil’d of his nose, and shorten’d of his ears.

s: Deiphobus's murder occurs during the destruction of Troy (when the Greek horse enters the city)
q: For, when the fatal horse, descending down, Pregnant with arms, o’erwhelm’d th’ unhappy town

s: Fate determine the judgment of souls (in the Underworld)
q: Fate, and the dooming gods, are deaf to tears.

s: Fate allow Aeneas's underworld journey (for a limited time)
q: And they, perhaps, in words and tears had spent The little time of stay which Heav’n had lent;

s: death forms their sentry
q: Here Toils, and Death, and Death’s half-brother, Sleep, Forms terrible to view, their sentry keep;

s: Sleep is a death's half-brother
q: Here Toils, and Death, and Death’s half-brother, Sleep,

s: the judgment of souls is conducted by Minos (with assessors)
q: Minos, the strict inquisitor, appears; And lives and crimes, with his assessors, hears.

s: the judgment of souls determines the fate of the dead (according to their crimes)
q: Round in his urn the blended balls he rolls, Absolves the just, and dooms the guilty souls.

s: Aeneas undertakes Aeneas's underworld journey (to seek Anchises)
q: Is sent to seek his sire in your Elysian grove.

s: punishment in Tartarus includes rolling a stone (for the condemned)
q: Some roll a weighty stone; some, laid along, And bound with burning wires, on spokes of wheels are hung

s: punishment in Tartarus includes eternal confinement (for Theseus)
q: Unhappy Theseus, doom’d for ever there, Is fix’d by fate on his eternal chair;

s: sin and justice are proclaimed by Phlegyas (as a warning to the living)
q: And wretched Phlegyas warns the world with cries (Could warning make the world more just or wise): ‘Learn righteousness, and dread th’ avenging deities.’

s: Aeneas visits the Underworld (while living)
q: But answer you; and in your turn relate, What brought you, living, to the Stygian state:

s: Aeneas meets Palinurus (among the dead)
q: Amidst the spirits, Palinurus press’d,

s: the happy souls is a souls (dwelling in the blessed afterlife)
q: Where long extended plains of pleasure lay: The verdant fields with those of heav’n may vie, With ether vested, and a purple sky; The blissful seats of happy souls below.

s: Troy is founded by the founder of Troy (whose identity is referenced among the honored dead)
q: Perpetual fame, with him who founded Troy.

s: Sibyl of Cumae addresses divine Musaeus (to ask for Anchises’ location)
q: To these the Sibyl thus her speech address’d, And first to him surrounded by the rest Tow’ring his height, and ample was his breast; “Say, happy souls, divine Musaeus, say, Where lives Anchises, and where lies our way

s: Anchises reviews his muster’d race (in a flow’ry vale)
q: But old Anchises, in a flow’ry vale, Review’d his muster’d race, and took the tale:

s: Anchises welcomes Aeneas (with open arms and tears)
q: He, when Aeneas on the plain appears, Meets him with open arms, and falling tears. “Welcome,” he said, “the gods’ undoubted race!

s: Aeneas is a son of Anchises (filially devoted)
q: To this, the filial duty thus replies:

s: Aeneas is descended from the gods (as part of Anchises’ race)
q: “Welcome,” he said, “the gods’ undoubted race!

s: the happy souls reside in groves (by crystal streams and in mossy beds)
q: In no fix’d place the happy souls reside. In groves we live, and lie on mossy beds, By crystal streams, that murmur thro’ the meads:

s: Aeneas is shown the future Italian race (by Anchises in the afterlife)
q: Thus having said, the father spirit leads The priestess and his son thro’ swarms of shades, And takes a rising ground, from thence to see The long procession of his progeny.

s: Lethe leads her silent flood (before the confines of the wood)
q: And, just before the confines of the wood, The gliding Lethe leads her silent flood.

s: Lethe causes forgetting past lives (through its waters)
q: In Lethe’s lake they long oblivion taste, Of future life secure, forgetful of the past.

s: the future Italian race is a progeny of Aeneas (destined to join the Trojan line)
q: These are th’ Italian names, which fate will join With ours, and graff upon the Trojan line.

s: the future Italian race awaits future bodies (before rebirth)
q: Those happy spirits, which, ordain’d by fate, For future beings and new bodies wait.

s: Silvius is bred by Lavinia (in groves)
q: Him fair Lavinia, thy surviving wife, Shall breed in groves, to lead a solitary life.

s: Lavinia is a surviving wife of Aeneas (mother of Silvius)
q: Him fair Lavinia, thy surviving wife, Shall breed in groves, to lead a solitary life.

s: Elysian plains is a blessed afterlife realm (where purified souls dwell)
q: The few, so cleans’d, to these abodes repair, And breathe, in ample fields, the soft Elysian air.

s: Romulus is born to restore the crown that once his injur’d grandsire wore
q: See Romulus the great, born to restore The crown that once his injur’d grandsire wore.

s: Romulus is born from a priestess of Trojan blood (with divine ancestry)
q: This prince a priestess of your blood shall bear, And like his sire in arms he shall appear. Two rising crests, his royal head adorn; Born from a god, himself to godhead born:

s: Romulus becomes a god god (for the skies)
q: Born from a god, himself to godhead born: His sire already signs him for the skies, And marks the seat amidst the deities.

s: Rome be imperial imperial
q: Auspicious chief! thy race, in times to come, Shall spread the conquests of imperial Rome.

s: Rome rules the world (through conquest and imperial power)
q: Rome, whose ascending tow’rs shall heav’n invade, Involving earth and ocean in her shade;

s: Julius Caesar awaits his promised power (impatiently)
q: The mighty Caesar waits his vital hour, Impatient for the world, and grasps his promis’d pow’r.

s: Augustus is a Caesar (exalted in the Julian line)
q: But next behold the youth of form divine, Caesar himself, exalted in his line; Augustus, promis’d oft, and long foretold,

s: Augustus restores the golden age (in Saturn’s former realm)
q: Sent to the realm that Saturn rul’d of old; Born to restore a better age of gold.

s: Augustus rules Africa (as part of his worldwide dominion)
q: Afric and India shall his pow’r obey;

s: the happy souls exercise their airy limbs (in sports)
q: Their airy limbs in sports they exercise, And on the green contend the wrestler’s prize.

s: Augustus rules India (as part of his worldwide dominion)
q: Afric and India shall his pow’r obey;

s: Augustus threatens Caspian kingdoms (with his approaching war)
q: At his foreseen approach, already quake The Caspian kingdoms and Maeotian lake:

s: Augustus threatens Maeotian lake (with his approaching war)
q: At his foreseen approach, already quake The Caspian kingdoms and Maeotian lake:

s: Augustus causes fear in Nile (at his approach)
q: Nile hears him knocking at his sev’nfold gates, And seeks his hidden spring, and fears his nephew’s fates.

s: Roman imperial rule rules mankind (through peace and war)
q: But, Rome, ’tis thine alone, with awful sway, To rule mankind, and make the world obey, Disposing peace and war by thy own majestic way;

s: Roman imperial rule frees the fetter’d slave (as an imperial art)
q: To tame the proud, the fetter’d slave to free: These are imperial arts, and worthy thee.”

s: Marcellus be rich with regal spoils
q: See great Marcellus! how, untir’d in toils, He moves with manly grace, how rich with regal spoils!

s: Marcellus defeats the Punic bands (more than once)
q: He, when his country, threaten’d with alarms, Requires his courage and his conqu’ring arms, Shall more than once the Punic bands affright;

s: Marcellus kills the Gaulish king (in single combat)
q: Shall kill the Gaulish king in single fight;

s: the younger Marcellus be shown on earth (for a day)
q: This youth (the blissful vision of a day) Shall just be shown on earth, and snatch’d away.

s: the happy souls sing heroic verse (divinely)
q: Some in heroic verse divinely sing;

s: the younger Marcellus is admired as the Trojan honour (after death)
q: The Trojan honour, and the Roman boast, Admir’d when living, and ador’d when lost!

s: the younger Marcellus have a funeral pyre flaming pile (in the Martian field)
q: What groans of men shall fill the Martian field! How fierce a blaze his flaming pile shall yield!

s: the younger Marcellus be seen by Tiber (at the sad solemnity)
q: What fun’ral pomp shall floating Tiber see, When, rising from his bed, he views the sad solemnity!

s: war are ordained by fate (for the Roman and Latin state)
q: Thus having said, he led the hero round The confines of the blest Elysian ground; Which when Anchises to his son had shown, And fir’d his mind to mount the promis’d throne, He tells the future wars, ordain’d by fate;

s: the Roman state has strength and customs (foretold by Anchises)
q: He tells the future wars, ordain’d by fate; The strength and customs of the Latian state;

s: Aeneas departs through the gate of ivory (with the Sibyl after Anchises’ prophecy)
q: Then, thro’ the gate of iv’ry, he dismiss’d His valiant offspring and divining guest.

s: Aeneas commands the ships (after leaving the underworld)
q: Straight to the ships Aeneas took his way, Embark’d his men, and skimm’d along the sea,

s: the ships reaches Cajeta’s bay (while coasting the Italian shore)
q: Still coasting, till he gain’d Cajeta’s bay.

s: Latinus is descended from Faunus (son of Faunus)
q: His father Faunus; a Laurentian dame His mother; fair Marica was her name.

s: Latinus is descended from Marica (son of Marica)
q: His father Faunus; a Laurentian dame His mother; fair Marica was her name.

s: Latinus is descended from Picus (through Faunus)
q: But Faunus came from Picus: Picus drew His birth from Saturn, if records be true. Thus King Latinus, in the third degree, Had Saturn author of his family

s: Latinus is descended from Saturn (through Picus and Faunus)
q: But Faunus came from Picus: Picus drew His birth from Saturn, if records be true. Thus King Latinus, in the third degree, Had Saturn author of his family

s: Latinus rules Latium (as king)
q: Latinus, old and mild, had long possess’d The Latin scepter, and his people blest:

s: Latinus receives the embassy to Latinus (at his palace)
q: In this high temple, on a chair of state, The seat of audience, old Latinus sate; Then gave admission to the Trojan train;

s: Latinus offers land to the Trojans (with ample leave to use his kingdom)
q: Have what you ask; your presents I receive; Land, where and when you please, with ample leave; Partake and use my kingdom as your own; All shall be yours, while I command the crown:

s: Turnus is a neighbouring prince (chief rival for Lavinia)
q: The neighb’ring princes court her nuptial bed. Among the crowd, but far above the rest, Young Turnus to the beauteous maid address’d.

s: Cajeta is buried in Hesperia (after her death)
q: Here rest thy bones in rich Hesperia’s plains;

s: Turnus addresses the beauteous maid
q: Among the crowd, but far above the rest, Young Turnus to the beauteous maid address’d.

s: Turnus is favoured by the Latian queen (because of high descent and graceful appearance)
q: Turnus, for high descent and graceful mien, Was first, and favour’d by the Latian queen;

s: Lavinia is a heiress (of Latinus’s crown and state)
q: His sons in blooming youth were snatch’d by fate; One only daughter heir’d the royal state.

s: Lavinia is destined to marry Aeneas (as a foreign bridegroom decreed by fate)
q: This was the foreign prince, by fate decreed To share his scepter, and Lavinia’s bed;

s: Lavinia is foretold to cause war (through her marriage and fate)
q: The nymph, who scatters flaming fires around, Shall shine with honour, shall herself be crown’d; But, caus’d by her irrevocable fate, War shall the country waste, and change the state.

s: Ascanius identifies the cakes used as trenchers (as an omen)
q: Ascanius this observ’d, and smiling said: “See, we devour the plates on which we fed.”

s: Aeneas is a Trojan prince (leader of the Trojan exiles)
q: The captain gives command; the joyful train Glide thro’ the gloomy shade, and leave the main.

s: Aeneas recognizes the Trojan arrival in Latium (as the fulfillment of Anchises’s prophecy)
q: This was that famine, this the fatal place Which ends the wand’ring of our exil’d race.

s: the Trojans are exiles from Troy (driven out by war)
q: From our sweet homes and ancient realms expell’d; Great as the greatest that the sun beheld.

s: the Trojans seek admission to Latium (peacefully)
q: And hither are we come, by his command, To crave admission in your happy land.

s: the Trojans build Trojan camp (with ramparts and palisades)
q: The Trojans round the place a rampire cast, And palisades about the trenches plac’d.

s: the embassy to Latinus is composed of the Trojans (one hundred youths)
q: A hundred youths from all his train selects, And to the Latian court their course directs,

s: Juno opposes the Trojan arrival in Latium (with enduring hatred and envy)
q: But jealous Juno, from Pachynus’ height, As she from Argos took her airy flight, Beheld with envious eyes this hateful sight.

s: Juno seeks to delay the proposed marriage of Aeneas and Lavinia (by prolonging war)
q: At least I can defer the nuptial day, And with protracted wars the peace delay:

s: Fate decree the proposed marriage of Aeneas and Lavinia (as inevitable)
q: This was the foreign prince, by fate decreed To share his scepter, and Lavinia’s bed;

s: Fate decree the Trojan rule in Italy (through the Trojan race)
q: Grant that the Fates have firm’d, by their decree, The Trojan race to reign in Italy;

s: the prophecies and portents be divulged by the king (in the silent night)
q: These answers, in the silent night receiv’d, The king himself divulg’d, the land believ’d: The fame thro’ all the neighb’ring nations flew, When now the Trojan navy was in view.

s: Neptune steers the Trojans (away from Circe’s enchanted coast)
q: Which monsters lest the Trojans’ pious host Should bear, or touch upon th’ inchanted coast, Propitious Neptune steer’d their course by night

s: Tiber flows through a wood (betwixt the trees)
q: The Trojan, from the main, beheld a wood, Which thick with shades and a brown horror stood: Betwixt the trees the Tiber took his course

s: Latinus is a king (old and mild ruler of the Latins)
q: Latinus, old and mild, had long possess’d The Latin scepter, and his people blest:

s: Juno is a goddess (divine queen)
q: Then Juno thus: “The grateful work is done, The seeds of discord sow’d, the war begun;

s: Alecto hides her hated head (in this infernal lake)
q: To this infernal lake the Fury flies; Here hides her hated head, and frees the lab’ring skies.

s: Amata is mother of Lavinia (as the royal mother)
q: If nature plead not in a parent’s heart, Pity my tears, and pity her desert.

s: Amata leads the madding matrons (in Bacchic rites)
q: She flies the town, and, mixing with a throng Of madding matrons, bears the bride along,

s: Amata advocates for Turnus (as Lavinia’s former betrothed)
q: And think on Turnus, her once plighted lord:

s: Turnus fights in fighting fields
q: Shall Turnus then such endless toil sustain In fighting fields, and conquer towns in vain?

s: Turnus is betrothed to Lavinia (formerly)
q: And think on Turnus, her once plighted lord:

s: Turnus resides in his lofty palace
q: Here, in his lofty palace, Turnus lay,

s: Juno commands Alecto (to foment war)
q: Her Juno finds, and thus inflames her spite: “O virgin daughter of eternal Night, Give me this once thy labour, to sustain My right, and execute my just disdain.

s: Latinus is a king (of Latium)
q: The Latian king, unless he shall submit, Own his old promise, and his new forget;

s: Latinus opposes war (at first, by refusing to open the gates)
q: These rites, of old by sov’reign princes us’d, Were the king’s office; but the king refus’d, Deaf to their cries, nor would the gates unbar Of sacred peace, or loose th’ imprison’d war;

s: Ascanius participates in the hunting match (with horns and hounds)
q: Where fair Ascanius and his youthful train, With horns and hounds, a hunting match ordain,

s: Ascanius participates in the hunting match (with his youthful companions)
q: Where fair Ascanius and his youthful train, With horns and hounds, a hunting match ordain,

s: Tyrrheus is foster father of the household stag (as keeper of the beast)
q: Tyrrheus, the foster father of the beast,

s: Juno favors Turnus (as his divine protector)
q: I neither fear nor will provoke the war; My fate is Juno’s most peculiar care.

s: the Trojans lands on the shore
q: The Phrygian fleet is landed on the shore.

s: the Rutuli prepares arms for war
q: The gods invok’d, the Rutuli prepare Their arms, and warn each other to the war.

s: Ardea is a city (formerly fair, now decayed)
q: ’Twas Ardua once; now Ardea’s name it bears; Once a fair city, now consum’d with years.

s: war is a conflict (between the Trojans and Ausonians)
q: The discord is complete; nor can they cease The dire debate, nor you command the peace.

s: war is begun by Alecto (through discord and bloodshed)
q: Behold! It is done, The blood already drawn, the war begun;

s: peace is a sacred condition (opposed to war)
q: Of sacred peace, or loose th’ imprison’d war;

s: the household stag uses the woodland grounds
q: This household beast, that us’d the woodland grounds,

s: Juno opens the gates of Mars (to release war)
q: Then heav’n’s imperious queen shot down from high: At her approach the brazen hinges fly; The gates are forc’d, and ev’ry falling bar; And, like a tempest, issues out the war.

s: the household stag is fostered by Tyrrheus (as a household animal)
q: Tyrrheus, the foster father of the beast,

s: the gates of Mars contain war (imprisoned until released)
q: nor would the gates unbar Of sacred peace, or loose th’ imprison’d war;

s: Styx arises in the sacred wood (in the centre)
q: Full in the centre of the sacred wood An arm arises of the Stygian flood,

s: Alecto is a Fury (infernal)
q: This Fury, fit for her intent, she chose;

s: Alecto is a daughter of eternal Night
q: “O virgin daughter of eternal Night,

s: Alecto is a sister of the Furies (hideous and feared)
q: Ev’n Pluto hates his own misshapen race; Her sister Furies fly her hideous face;

s: Alecto carries war, death, destruction (in my hand)
q: War, death, destruction, in my hand I bear.”

s: Mezentius appears on the plain
q: Mezentius first appear’d upon the plain:

s: Turnus bears shield (decorated with Io and the river god)
q: Fair Io grac’d his shield; but Io now With horns exalted stands, and seems to low— A noble charge! Her keeper by her side, To watch her walks, his hundred eyes applied; And on the brims her sire, the wat’ry god, Roll’d from a silver urn his crystal flood.

s: Aventinus is a son of Hercules (of divine and mortal blood)
q: The son of Hercules he justly seems By his broad shoulders and gigantic limbs; Of heav’nly part, and part of earthly blood, A mortal woman mixing with a god.

s: Aventinus is the son of Hercules
q: The son of Hercules he justly seems

s: Aventinus is born of Rhea (through Hercules’ union with her)
q: Then on Mount Aventine the son of Jove The priestess Rhea found, and forc’d to love.

s: Aventinus wears lion skin (as a savage, Hercules-like dress)
q: Like Hercules himself his son appears, In salvage pomp; a lion’s hide he wears;

s: Hercules slays Geryon (the triple Geryon)
q: For strong Alcides, after he had slain The triple Geryon, drove from conquer’d Spain His captive herds;

s: Mezentius brings his baffled host (to Turnus’ aid)
q: Etruria lost, He brings to Turnus’ aid his baffled host.

s: Praeneste has founder Vulcan (according to report)
q: Nor was Praeneste’s founder wanting there, Whom fame reports the son of Mulciber:

s: Messapus is a son of Neptune (secure from steel and destined to survive fire)
q: Messapus next, (great Neptune was his sire,) Secure of steel, and fated from the fire,

s: Messapus commands Faliscans (in battle)
q: The just Faliscans he to battle brings,

s: Neptune is the sire of Messapus (divine father)
q: Messapus next, (great Neptune was his sire,)

s: Clausus leads Sabine land (a numerous embodied force)
q: Then Clausus came, who led a num’rous band Of troops embodied from the Sabine land,

s: Clausus is the ancestor of Claudian race (progenitor of the future imperial family)
q: ’Twas he, the noble Claudian race begot, The Claudian race, ordain’d, in times to come, To share the greatness of imperial Rome.

s: Claudian race is destined to share the greatness of Rome (in times to come)
q: The Claudian race, ordain’d, in times to come, To share the greatness of imperial Rome.

s: Halesus is a foe of Troy (by birth)
q: High in his chariot then Halesus came, A foe by birth to Troy’s unhappy name:

s: Halesus is the son of Agamemnon (a youthful hero)
q: From Agamemnon born—to Turnus’ aid A thousand men the youthful hero led,

s: Halesus leads army (a thousand men to Turnus’ aid)
q: From Agamemnon born—to Turnus’ aid A thousand men the youthful hero led,

s: Mezentius is the sire of Lausus (an unworthy father of a brave son)
q: His sire unworthy of so brave a son; Himself well worthy of a happier throne.

s: Ufens is a leader (leader of the mountain troops from Nursia)
q: Next these in rank, the warlike Ufens went, And led the mountain troops that Nursia sent.

s: Ufens rules Equicolae (whose customs are hunting and plundering)
q: The rude Equicolae his rule obey’d; Hunting their sport, and plund’ring was their trade.

s: Umbro is a priest (leader of the Marrubians)
q: Umbro the priest the proud Marrubians led,

s: Umbro is sent by Archippus (to aid Turnus)
q: By King Archippus sent to Turnus’ aid,

s: Umbro possesses healing arts (can calm vipers and serpent wounds with wand, words, and herbs)
q: His wand and holy words, the viper’s rage, And venom’d wounds of serpents could assuage. He, when he pleas’d with powerful juice to steep Their temples, shut their eyes in pleasing sleep.

s: Lausus is a warrior (youthful and skilful in horsemanship and hunting)
q: The charming Lausus, full of youthful fire, Rode in the rank, and next his sullen sire; To Turnus only second in the grace Of manly mien, and features of the face. A skilful horseman, and a huntsman bred,

s: Hippolytus is a hunter (unhappily killed by wild horses)
q: Torn by wild horses on the sandy shore, Another’s crimes th’ unhappy hunter bore,

s: Hippolytus is restored by Diana (with Aesculapian herbs after death)
q: But chaste Diana, who his death deplor’d, With Aesculapian herbs his life restor’d.

s: Virbius is a son of Hippolytus (the second Virbius and a warrior)
q: His son, the second Virbius, yet retain’d His father’s art, and warrior steeds he rein’d.

s: Virbius is born in Aricia (son of Hippolytus and Aricia)
q: The son of fam’d Hippolytus was there, Fam’d as his sire, and, as his mother, fair; Whom in Egerian groves Aricia bore, And nurs’d his youth along the marshy shore,

s: Virbius retains his father’s art
q: His son, the second Virbius, yet retain’d His father’s art, and warrior steeds he rein’d.

s: Camilla is a warrior dame (leader of the Volscian troops)
q: Last, from the Volscians fair Camilla came, And led her warlike troops, a warrior dame;

s: Camilla is unskilled in spinning (she rejects domestic labor)
q: Unbred to spinning, in the loom unskill’d, She chose the nobler Pallas of the field.

s: Camilla chooses the nobler Pallas of the field
q: Unbred to spinning, in the loom unskill’d, She chose the nobler Pallas of the field.

s: Camilla possesses myrtle javelin (carried in battle)
q: She shakes her myrtle jav’lin; and, behind, Her Lycian quiver dances in the wind.

s: Camilla possesses Lycian quiver (worn behind her in battle)
q: She shakes her myrtle jav’lin; and, behind, Her Lycian quiver dances in the wind.

s: Lausus leads army (a thousand men)
q: With fates averse a thousand men he led:

s: Volscians are led by Camilla (in war)
q: Last, from the Volscians fair Camilla came, And led her warlike troops, a warrior dame;

s: Camilla’s warrior band is a army (warlike troops led by Camilla)
q: Last, from the Volscians fair Camilla came, And led her warlike troops, a warrior dame;

s: war is characterized by arms (including swords, spears, and clattering shields)
q: A cloud of foot succeeds, and fills the fields With swords, and pointed spears, and clatt’ring shields;

s: Lausus is worthy of happier throne
q: His sire unworthy of so brave a son; Himself well worthy of a happier throne.

s: Turnus is above the rest (in arms)
q: Amid the troops, and like the leading god, High o’er the rest in arms the graceful Turnus rode:

s: Turnus wears triple of plumes (on his crest)
q: A triple of plumes his crest adorn’d,

s: war is a war
q: When Turnus had assembled all his pow’rs, His standard planted on Laurentum’s tow’rs; When now the sprightly trumpet, from afar, Had giv’n the signal of approaching war,

s: Ascanius builds Rome (after thirty rolling years, according to the prophecy)
q: When thirty rolling years have run their race, Thy son Ascanius, on this empty space, Shall build a royal town, of lasting fame,

s: Aeneas sacrifices fatal white sow (with her thirty piglets on Juno’s altar)
q: Aeneas takes the mother and her brood, And all on Juno’s altar are bestow’d.

s: Aeneas’s journey to Evander ends at Evander’s kingdom
q: These cots (Evander’s kingdom, mean and poor) The Trojan saw, and turn’d his ships to shore.

s: Pallanteum is a Arcadian settlement (founded by Evander)
q: A banish’d band, Driv’n with Evander from th’ Arcadian land, Have planted here, and plac’d on high their walls; Their town the founder Pallanteum calls,

s: Evander has kingdom Evander’s kingdom
q: These cots (Evander’s kingdom, mean and poor)

s: Pallas is a son of Evander
q: Betwixt young Pallas and his aged sire, The Trojan pass’d, the city to survey,

s: Pallas welcomes Aeneas (after Aeneas announces peaceful intentions)
q: Struck with so great a name, and all on fire, The youth replies: “Whatever you require, Your fame exacts. Upon our shores descend. A welcome guest, and, what you wish, a friend.”

s: Evander offers the league (as your right)
q: The league you ask, I offer, as your right; And, when tomorrow’s sun reveals the light, With swift supplies you shall be sent away.

s: Evander is a king
q: The king and prince, without the city gates, Then paid their off’rings in a sacred grove

s: the Trojan people are expelled from Troy (and opposed in Italy by Latian foes)
q: The Phrygians’ arms you see, Expell’d from Troy, provok’d in Italy By Latian foes, with war unjustly made;

s: Rutulians oppose the Trojan people (with an unjust war in Italy)
q: The Phrygians’ arms you see, Expell’d from Troy, provok’d in Italy By Latian foes, with war unjustly made;

s: Arcadians is planted in here (driven with Evander from the Arcadian land)
q: A banish’d band, Driv’n with Evander from th’ Arcadian land, Have planted here, and plac’d on high their walls;

s: Hercules festival honors Hercules (with annual rites)
q: From that auspicious day, with rites divine, We worship at the hero’s holy shrine. Potitius first ordain’d these annual vows:

s: Hercules is a son of Jupiter (warrior hero)
q: To Hercules, the warrior son of Jove.

s: Hercules binds the monster
q: The wrathful god then plunges from above, And, where in thickest waves the sparkles drove, There lights; and wades thro’ fumes, and gropes his way, Half sing’d, half stifled, till he grasps his prey. The monster, spewing fruitless flames, he found; He squeez’d his throat; he writh’d his neck around, And in a knot his crippled members bound;

s: Cacus possesses This hold (more than half a beast)
q: The monster Cacus, more than half a beast, This hold, impervious to the sun, possess’d.

s: Turnus sends for aid to Diomede (to defend Ausonia)
q: Then Venulus to Diomede they send, To beg his aid Ausonia to defend,

s: Cacus is a son of Vulcan (fire-breathing monster)
q: Vulcan this plague begot; and, like his sire, Black clouds he belch’d, and flakes of livid fire.

s: Cacus’s cave is a rocky den (deep beneath the ground and impervious to the sun)
q: ’Twas once a robber’s den, inclos’d around With living stone, and deep beneath the ground. The monster Cacus, more than half a beast, This hold, impervious to the sun, possess’d.

s: Hercules’s slaying of Cacus commemorated by rites divine (from that auspicious day)
q: From that auspicious day, with rites divine, We worship at the hero’s holy shrine.

s: Hercules’s cattle are stolen by Cacus (four oxen and four cows)
q: The brutal Cacus, as by chance they stray’d, Four oxen thence, and four fair kine convey’d;

s: Hercules drives Hercules’s cattle (near Tiber’s bank after returning from Spain)
q: Th’ avenging force of Hercules, from Spain, Arriv’d in triumph, from Geryon slain: Thrice liv’d the giant, and thrice liv’d in vain. His prize, the lowing herds, Alcides drove Near Tiber’s bank, to graze the shady grove.

s: Potitius ordains Hercules festival (as the first keeper of its annual vows)
q: Potitius first ordain’d these annual vows:

s: Salii censes Hercules
q: The Salii sing, and cense his altars round With Saban smoke, their heads with poplar bound

s: Rome is washed by Tiber (in times to come)
q: This is my certain seat. In times to come, My waves shall wash the walls of mighty Rome.

s: Venulus is a messenger (sent to Diomede)
q: Then Venulus to Diomede they send, To beg his aid Ausonia to defend,

s: Aeneas is a Trojan leader
q: The Trojan chief Was laid on Tiber’s banks, oppress’d with grief,

s: Aeneas relies on their aid (against the fierce Latians)
q: A banish’d band, Driv’n with Evander from th’ Arcadian land, Have planted here, and plac’d on high their walls; Their town the founder Pallanteum calls, Deriv’d from Pallas, his great-grandsire’s name: But the fierce Latians old possession claim, With war infesting the new colony. These make thy friends, and on their aid rely.

s: Tiber is a river god (whose waters flow around the fields)
q: The god am I, whose yellow water flows Around these fields, and fattens as it goes: Tiber my name; among the rolling floods Renown’d on earth, esteem’d among the gods.

s: Tiber is seated at Tiber (as his certain seat)
q: This is my certain seat. In times to come, My waves shall wash the walls of mighty Rome.

s: Venus is a goddess (love goddess)
q: When love’s fair goddess, anxious for her son,

s: Aeneas is a Trojan prince (survivor of Troy)
q: Undaunted prince, I never can believe The Trojan empire lost, while you survive.

s: Aeneas is son of Venus (divine parentage)
q: My goddess mother, whose indulgent care Foresaw the dangers of the growing war,

s: Aeneas is destined to rule Italy (by Jove’s command and fate’s decree)
q: But now, by Jove’s command, and fate’s decree, His race is doom’d to reign in Italy:

s: Aeneas leads the Trojan people (in war)
q: The horsemen march; the gates are open’d wide; Aeneas at their head, Achates by his side.

s: Aeneas wages war (for the future of his people)
q: Turnus shall dearly pay for faith forsworn;

s: Aeneas receives divine omen of the armor (as a sign of promised aid)
q: Heav’n calls me to the war: th’ expected sign Is giv’n of promis’d aid, and arms divine.

s: Turnus is an enemy of Aeneas (in the Italian war)
q: Now seek, secure, the Latian enemy, And haughty Turnus to the field defy.”

s: Evander is a king (Arcadian king)
q: Then, to th’ Arcadian king: “This prodigy

s: Evander is father of Pallas (father and son)
q: Young Pallas did his father’s steps attend,

s: Venus is mother of Aeneas (divine mother)
q: A mother kneels a suppliant for her son.

s: Evander allies with Aeneas (against the Latins)
q: Their num’rous troops, now muster’d on the strand, My counsel shall submit to your command.

s: Evander declines rule of Tuscans (because of age and declining strength)
q: But the chill blood that creeps within my veins, And age, and listless limbs unfit for pains, And a soul conscious of its own decay, Have forc’d me to refuse imperial sway.

s: Pallas commands 200 horse (a chosen band)
q: Besides, two hundred horse he shall command; Tho’ few, a warlike and well-chosen band.

s: Pallas is partly Sabine (through his mother)
q: And should, but he’s a Sabine mother’s son, And half a native;

s: Mezentius is a tyrant (of Caere)
q: Till curs’d Mezentius, in a fatal hour, Assum’d the crown, with arbitrary pow’r.

s: Mezentius rules Caere (as an arbitrary king)
q: Till curs’d Mezentius, in a fatal hour, Assum’d the crown, with arbitrary pow’r.

s: Mezentius flees to Turnus (after revolt in Caere)
q: He cleaves the crowd, and, favour’d by the night, To Turnus’ friendly court directs his flight.

s: Troy is destroyed by the Greeks (in war)
q: While cruel fate conspir’d with Grecian pow’rs, To level with the ground the Trojan tow’rs,

s: Venus couches with her husband (in his golden bed)
q: Couch’d with her husband in his golden bed,

s: Italy is destined to be ruled by Aeneas (through his race)
q: His race is doom’d to reign in Italy:

s: Tiber bounds Arcadians (on one side of their kingdom)
q: Our narrow kingdom here the Tiber bounds;

s: Tiber bears dead bodies and weapons (as a consequence of war)
q: And corps, and swords, and shields, on Tiber borne, Shall choke his flood:

s: the Trojan people are relics of the Phrygian kind
q: Behold, what haughty nations are combin’d Against the relics of the Phrygian kind,

s: Arcadians are led by Evander (as their king)
q: Then, to th’ Arcadian king: “This prodigy

s: Tuscans revolt against Mezentius (because of his tyranny)
q: The people’s patience, tir’d, no longer bore The raging monster; but with arms beset His house, and vengeance and destruction threat.

s: Tuscans seeks a foreign head (to lead this pow’rful people)
q: Know this: no native of our land may lead This pow’rful people; seek a foreign head.’

s: Tuscans are led by Tarchon (as chief)
q: Not far from hence, along the river’s side, In tents secure, the Tuscan troops abide, By Tarchon led.

s: Venus does not request aid (to restore the unhappy)
q: I ask’d not aid th’ unhappy to restore, Nor did the succour of thy skill implore;

s: Romans are led by Young Caesar (in armour bright)
q: Young Caesar, on the stern, in armour bright, Here leads the Romans and their gods to fight:

s: Romans triumphs Rome
q: The victor to the gods his thanks express’d, And Rome, triumphant, with his presence bless’d.

s: shield of Aeneas depicts Roman history (in embossed scenes)
q: But most admires the shield’s mysterious mould, And Roman triumphs rising on the gold:

s: shield of Aeneas depicts rape of the Sabine women (as an episode of Roman history)
q: Not far from thence new Rome appears, with games Projected for the rape of Sabine dames.

s: war is supported by Vulcan’s armor for Aeneas (divinely forged weapons)
q: Heav’n calls me to the war: th’ expected sign Is giv’n of promis’d aid, and arms divine.

s: Fate determines Aeneas’s rule in Italy (by divine decree)
q: But now, by Jove’s command, and fate’s decree, His race is doom’d to reign in Italy:

s: divine omen of the armor signals war (as promised divine aid)
q: This prodigy (Dismiss your fear) belongs alone to me. Heav’n calls me to the war: th’ expected sign Is giv’n of promis’d aid, and arms divine.

s: Vulcan is husband of Venus (married relationship)
q: Couch’d with her husband in his golden bed,

s: Vulcan commands the Cyclopes (at the forge)
q: “My sons,” said Vulcan, “set your tasks aside; Your strength and master-skill must now be tried.

s: Vulcan’s armor for Aeneas is Vulcan’s labour’d art
q: Behold,” she said, “perform’d in ev’ry part, My promise made, and Vulcan’s labour’d art.

s: Turnus is a Daunian hero
q: The Daunian hero lifts his hands and eyes,

s: Jupiter is a ruler of heaven and earth
q: Then thus replied her awful son, who rolls The radiant stars, and heav’n and earth controls:

s: Jupiter transforms fleet transformed into sea nymphs (after they reach the Latian shore)
q: Whatever ships escape the raging storms, At my command shall change their fading forms To nymphs divine, and plow the wat’ry way, Like Dotis and the daughters of the sea.”

s: fleet transformed into sea nymphs transforms into beauteous maids (like dolphins)
q: No sooner had the goddess ceas’d to speak, When, lo! th’ obedient ships their haulsers break; And, strange to tell, like dolphins, in the main They plunge their prows, and dive, and spring again: As many beauteous maids the billows sweep, As rode before tall vessels on the deep.

s: Trojan fleet lies beneath the Trojan camp walls (close underneath the walls and protected by the washing tide)
q: roams the nightly wolf about the fold: Wet with descending show’rs, and stiff with cold, He howls for hunger, and he grins for pain, (His gnashing teeth are exercis’d in vain,) And, impotent of anger, finds no way In his distended paws to grasp the prey. The mothers listen; but the bleating lambs Securely swig the dug, beneath the dams. Thus ranges eager Turnus o’er the plain. Sharp with desire, and furious with disdain; Surveys each passage with a piercing sight, To force his foes in equal field to fight. Thus while he gazes round, at length he spies, Where, fenc’d with strong redoubts, their navy lies, Close underneath the walls; the washing tide Secures from all approach this weaker side

s: burning of the Trojan ships uses kindled fires (against the fir’d pines)
q: He takes the wish’d occasion, fills his hand With ready fires, and shakes a flaming brand. Urg’d by his presence, ev’ry soul is warm’d, And ev’ry hand with kindled fires is arm’d. From the fir’d pines the scatt’ring sparkles fly; Fat vapours, mix’d with flames, involve the sky.

s: Trojan camp is defended by the Trojans (behind ramparts and gates)
q: The Trojans view the dusty cloud from far, And the dark menace of the distant war. Caicus from the rampire saw it rise, Black’ning the fields, and thick’ning thro’ the skies. Then to his fellows thus aloud he calls: “What rolling clouds, my friends, approach the walls? Arm! arm! and man the works! prepare your spears And pointed darts! the Latian host appears.” Thus warn’d, they shut their gates; with shouts ascend The bulwarks, and, secure, their foes attend:

s: the Trojans are besieged (within their fortified camp)
q: The post of honour to Messapus falls, To keep the nightly guard, to watch the walls, To pitch the fires at distances around, And close the Trojans in their scanty ground.

s: Nisus is a Trojan warrior (stationed on the night watch)
q: Nigh where the foes their utmost guards advance, To watch the gate was warlike Nisus’ chance.
